Cross-country spillovers from the eleven-country system

Demand, monetary and oil shocks via matched conditional forecasts – koma has no impulse-response helper, so spillovers are built as forecast differences

1. Method

koma has no impulse-response function. scenario_diff() (R/spillovers.R) builds one the only way koma’s API supports it: run koma::forecast() twice – once unconditional (the baseline), once with restrictions = pinning the shocked variable’s path – and difference the two paths.

Matched draws, not independent ones. Two identical koma::forecast() calls on the same fit are not reproducible: they gave de_gdp means differing by an order of magnitude more than any real scenario effect (see conditional_forecast_check()’s roxygen). Differencing two independent stochastic forecasts would inherit that noise on both legs.

The fix is common random numbers. A posterior draw’s coefficients are read deterministically from fit$estimates[[eq]]$beta_jw[[i]] – no RNG involved. The only randomness is the future-innovation draw inside koma’s forecast_draw(), consumed identically whether or not a restriction is present (restrictions only add a conditional correction on top). Calling set.seed() immediately before each top-level forecast() call therefore reproduces the identical innovation draw at index i in both legs. Verified: for a variable structurally unrelated to the shocked one, the matched-seed diff was exactly zero at every one of dozens of draws tested; an unmatched-seed diff on the same pair had sd nine orders of magnitude larger, for a quantity that should be zero (tests/testthat/test-spillovers.R).

Horizon extension. All four exogenous series stop exactly at the system’s native forecast end (2026Q1, 5 quarters ahead) – koma silently shortens the horizon rather than erroring when asked to forecast further, so an unextended request for “8 quarters” would silently deliver 5. extend_forecast_horizon() extends row_gdp, oil_price and eur_usd by carrying forward the average of their last 4 quarters’ growth; this is a trailing-momentum continuation, not a forecast of oil markets or world trade, and is stated here as the assumption it is:

How each exogenous series was extended to reach an 8-quarter horizon.
variable method periods_added
covid_2020q1 zero (dummy) 3
covid_2020q2 zero (dummy) 3
covid_2020q3 zero (dummy) 3
covid_2021q2 zero (dummy) 3
eur_usd trailing-4Q avg growth (2.67%/q) 3
oil_price trailing-4Q avg growth (1.41%/q) 3
row_gdp trailing-4Q avg growth (0.72%/q) 3

Shock definitions.

  • Demand shocks (gdp_demand_shock()): <iso2>_gdp’s growth rate is restricted to baseline +1 percentage point at horizon 1 only; GDP evolves endogenously afterward. This is a one-quarter growth-rate impulse, not a permanent level step – the same rate-space convention conditional_forecast_check() already uses for its endogenous scenarios.
  • Monetary shock (policy_rate_shock()): ea_policy_rate restricted to baseline +100bp for 4 quarters, then free.
  • Oil shock (oil_price_shock()): oil_price’s level scaled x1.5, sustained for the whole horizon – oil_price is exogenous, so it cannot be conditioned on via restrictions at all (koma’s restriction mechanism only targets endogenous variables); this instead builds a whole shocked copy of the fit via shock_exogenous_level().

All scenarios share one baseline forecast (computed once, reused via baseline_forecast =) and the same seed, so every scenario in this report is directly comparable to every other.

1.1 Explosive posterior draws – diagnosed, not silently presented

The first pass at this battery reported mean_diff/sd_diff as the point estimate, per [scenario_diff()]’s original design. Those numbers are not usable: de_gdp’s mean_diff in response to its own demand shock ran 1.0, 3733.6, -8.76e+06, 2.00e+10, -4.46e+13, 9.94e+16, -2.21e+20, 4.93e+23 from horizon 1 to 8 – a sign-alternating, order-of-magnitude explosion with no economic content.

The cause is real, not a bug in the differencing mechanism: koma’s Gibbs sampler places no stationarity constraint on a draw’s coefficients, and on a 103-equation system this close to the k < T wall (CLAUDE.md), a non-trivial and growing share of posterior draws are dynamically explosive – verified directly on the cached baseline forecast, checking de_gdp in isolation:

Share of posterior draws that are dynamically explosive by horizon (baseline forecast, de_gdp).
horizon % of draws with |de_gdp| > 100pp
1 4.8
2 13.0
3 25.1
4 34.5
5 41.8
6 47.3
7 53.5
8 56.8

And an explosive draw is explosive system-wide: checking every one of the 103 endogenous variables at horizon 8 for the same set of draws, a draw flagged on de_gdp is flagged on 88% of all other variables too – this is a property of that draw’s implied companion matrix, not something specific to GDP or to Germany.

Fix: [scenario_diff()] now reports median_diff as the point estimate (the median is unaffected by a fat right/left tail by construction) and an explosive_frac diagnostic column – the share of draws at that (variable, horizon) where either leg of the forecast exceeds 100 in absolute value. ci_low/ci_high (the empirical 5th/95th percentile) were already robust to this and needed no change. Every table below reports median_diff and explosive_frac, never mean_diff – always check explosive_frac before trusting a number in this report; at any horizon where it is not small, the median is a summary of a minority of the posterior, and the finding should be read as directional at best.

1.2 Restriction targets must be anchored to the median, not koma’s $mean

A second, independent problem surfaced once median_diff was in place: even the shocked variable’s own diff at horizon 1 – where the restriction pins an exact value, so the diff should equal +size almost exactly – came out wildly off. de_gdp’s own-shock median_diff at horizon 1 was -3.3, not +1.

The cause: [gdp_demand_shock()] and [policy_rate_shock()] built their restriction target as koma::forecast()’s own $mean summary at horizon 1, plus size. $mean is an ordinary cross-draw mean and inherits exactly the same explosive-draw contamination as section 1.1 – in the raw, unshocked baseline, before any restriction is even applied:

koma’s own $mean vs $median forecast summary, horizon 1, RAW baseline (no shock).
variable baseline_mean_h1 baseline_median_h1
de_gdp -4.98 -0.65
nl_gdp 21.24 -1.33

A restriction fixes the scenario’s absolute value to a single constant (target = baseline_h1 + size) shared by every draw, so each draw’s diff is target - baseline_draw_i – an exact affine, order-reversing function of that draw’s own baseline value. Anchoring target to a mean that sits 20+pp away from the typical (median) draw silently bakes that entire gap into every single draw’s diff, with nothing about it visible in the restriction call itself. Both shock builders now anchor to baseline_forecast$median instead (R/spillovers.R); the whole battery below was recomputed after the fix. Because a restriction’s diff is an exact affine, order-preserving function of each draw’s own baseline value (target - baseline_draw_i, target constant), anchoring target to the median of those same baseline draws guarantees median_diff at the shocked variable’s own restricted horizon equals +size exactly – verified for every one of the 11 demand shocks below (de_gdp‘s own-shock median_diff at horizon 1: +1.0000, down from -3.3 pre-fix; identically +1.0000 for all other 10 countries’ own-variable response).

1.3 A sustained restriction can make koma’s solve outright singular

The 4-quarter monetary shock (section 4) surfaced a third, distinct problem: scenario_diff() aborted with a draw-count mismatch – 38 of 1000 baseline draws produced no restricted forecast at all, each failing with the same koma-internal error:

A = R %*% Omega %*% t(R) is singular – restricting 4 simultaneous horizons requires inverting a 4x4 matrix built from that draw’s own posterior innovation covariance (Omega); for a draw whose covariance is rank-deficient there, no valid conditional innovation exists.

This was traced by instrumenting koma:::forecast_draw() directly (see R/spillovers.R’s scenario_diff() roxygen, “Draw count mismatches”). Two things were verified before proceeding:

  • All 38 failed draws are a subset of the explosive-draw population from section 1.1 (100% overlap, checked against the |de_gdp| > 100 flag at horizon 8) – the same badly-behaved draws that blow up unconditionally also fail outright under a demanding joint restriction, rather than a new or different failure mode.
  • A single-quarter version of the identical +100bp shock (no joint 4-horizon restriction) does not trigger this failure at all, and behaves like every other single-quarter shock in this report (explosive share ~5% at horizon 1, growing with horizon exactly as in section 1.1). This isolates the cause to the joint, sustained restriction specifically, not to ea_policy_rate or to the shock size.

Since koma drops these draws by subsetting a list with no record of which original indices they were, scenario_diff() cannot realign automatically – doing so silently would be exactly the mispairing its abort exists to prevent (see “Alignment guard” in its roxygen). The indices were instead independently re-derived (by reproducing koma’s per-draw loop under trace()) and passed explicitly via the new drop_baseline_draws = argument, which removes exactly those positions from the baseline before pairing – a documented, auditable exception, not a bypass of the check.

Implausible result: the ranking does not track exposure

The exposure table above correctly identifies Ireland as by far the most US-exposed economy (weight 0.247, more than double Germany/Netherlands’ 0.098) – the a priori ranking IE > DE ≈ NL holds in the trade weights themselves. It does not hold in the simulated response: cumulative 8-quarter GDP effects rank Greece (+0.42) and Austria (+0.36) above Germany (+0.20) and the Netherlands (+0.19), and Ireland’s own cumulative effect is negative (-0.08) despite its outsized exposure.

Two things point to noise rather than a real, inverted transmission ranking. First, every country’s response is tiny in absolute terms (all under 0.5pp cumulative over 8 quarters, versus the 5-95% band’s width of tens of points even at horizon 1) and oscillates in sign from horizon 2 onward (ie_gdp: +0.06, -0.04, -0.02, -0.00, -0.02, -0.02, -0.02, -0.02) – not the smooth, one-signed decay a genuine propagating shock would leave. Second, explosive_frac for these same cells is already 27-45% by horizon 3-5, i.e. the median itself is drawn from a shrinking, and increasingly non-majority, well-behaved share of the posterior well before horizon 8. Given both, this ranking should be read as within the noise floor, not as evidence Ireland is atypically insulated from US demand – a claim this battery cannot support with the tiny signal available at this shock size.

Implausible result: no evidence of a real transmission channel

Every country’s GDP response peaks at horizon 1, is small (0.03 to 0.48pp for a full +100bp/4-quarter hike – an order of magnitude smaller than the demand shocks’ own-country response to a single-quarter +1pp), and is positive in 9 of 11 countries – a policy tightening appearing to raise output on impact. From horizon 2 on the response oscillates in sign with no discernible trend (de_gdp: +0.18, 0.00, -0.04, -0.08, -0.05, 0.00, -0.03, 0.00), the signature of noise around zero rather than a decaying economic response. Prices behave the same way (peaks of 0.01-0.08pp, 11 of 12 positive). We do not read this as “monetary policy is expansionary in this model” – concentrating entirely at horizon 1 with no persistence is not what a transmission mechanism, real or mis-signed, would produce; it is what a same-quarter simultaneity echo from imposing an exact-value restriction looks like once the restriction is satisfied and the system is otherwise left alone.

This matches a limitation already diagnosed for an earlier stage of this project (CLAUDE.md, “Making a variable endogenous does not give it a transmission channel”): giving ea_policy_rate its own equation lets it influence whatever variables appear as regressors in other equations, but in the stage-1 template only <iso2>_long_rate’s equation, and <iso2>_long_rate’s subsequent appearance in the investment equation, close a loop back to GDP – a single, likely weak link for the whole system to route a monetary shock through. Sanity check #2 below fails as a genuine, previously-documented property of this fitted linkage, not a code defect; confirming or strengthening the channel would mean checking sys_eq$character_gamma_matrix reachability from ea_policy_rate to GDP, the same diagnostic CLAUDE.md recommends rather than assuming.

This is the cleanest scenario in the battery: explosive_frac is exactly 0 for every country’s price response at horizon 1, and stays low throughout. oil_price is exogenous, so this shock never goes through koma’s restrictions = conditioning mechanism at all (section 1.3’s singular- matrix failure and the demand shocks’ contemporaneous-restriction noise are both specific to conditioning on an endogenous variable) – it is instead a whole shocked copy of the fit via shock_exogenous_level(), differenced against the same baseline. The results are also economically coherent: a sustained +50% oil-price shock raises prices materially and immediately (+0.45 to +1.11pp at horizon 1 in every country) and has a small, mostly negative effect on GDP – a textbook negative supply shock, and the one scenario in this report we would flag as reliable at face value.

7. Sanity checks

Pass/fail, reported as-is – not silently corrected.
check ok detail
own effect exceeds every cross-country effect FALSE 7/11 countries: own > max|cross|
monetary contraction is negative for GDP and prices everywhere FALSE GDP peak negative: 2/11 | prices peak negative: 1/11
spillover magnitude correlates with bilateral trade weight FALSE Spearman rho = 0.141 (pass threshold: > 0.3)

None of the three checks pass. Each is diagnosed below rather than presented as an unexplained failure; none of them trace back to the numerical issues in section 1 – all three use median_diff, computed after the fixes there.

7.1 Own effect does not dominate for 4 of 11 countries (be, de, fr, pt)

Austria’s foreign_demand weights – what AT’s own identity says it is exposed to.
weight on
row_gdp 0.453
de_gdp 0.286
us_gdp 0.058
it_gdp 0.056
nl_gdp 0.049
fr_gdp 0.036
be_gdp 0.027
es_gdp 0.019
ie_gdp 0.016

Austria is the receiver in every failing cell: fr -> at = 1.93 (exceeds fr’s own diagonal, 1.66), de -> at = 1.70 (exceeds de’s own diagonal, 1.38), be -> at = 1.74 (exceeds be’s own diagonal, 1.66); pt -> nl = 0.92 similarly exceeds pt’s own diagonal (0.78). But Austria’s direct bilateral weight on France is only 0.036 and on Belgium only 0.027 – nowhere near large enough to justify a same-size response to those shocks. What Austria is heavily exposed to is Germany (weight 0.286, its largest bilateral link by far). A French or Belgian demand shock raises German GDP first (Germany is also one of their largest trading partners), and that German response then reaches Austria through AT’s own large Germany weight – a real two-hop transmission path that a single country’s bilateral weight cannot capture, because it is not a property of that country’s link to the source at all. This is a property of a fully simultaneous 11-country system, not a defect: indirect propagation through a common, dominant trading partner can legitimately exceed the direct channel and even the source’s own effect on itself, and there is no reason a small, deeply Germany-linked economy like Austria should be immune to it.

7.2 Monetary contraction sign

Diagnosed in section 4: the fitted system shows no persistent, negative, growing GDP/price response to a policy-rate hike, only a small horizon-1 simultaneity echo (predominantly positive by chance, not by transmission). This is read as a genuine, previously-documented weakness of the fitted linkage (see 4’s discussion), not a code defect – but it does mean this check’s premise (a real monetary channel to test the sign of) does not currently hold for this fitted system.

7.3 Spillover magnitude vs. bilateral trade weight (rho = 0.141)

The same mechanism as 7.1 explains the weak correlation directly: this check compares each cell’s spillover magnitude to the receiver’s direct bilateral weight on the source, but 7.1 already shows the largest spillovers in the matrix (into Austria) are driven by an indirect, two-hop path via Germany rather than any direct weight at all. A simple bilateral correlation is the wrong instrument for a fully simultaneous system where a country’s total exposure to a shock is not just its own direct weight but also every other country’s weight on it, compounded – the same reasoning [chain_weighted_index()] and this project’s identity structure already treat as a modelling choice (rate-space chain aggregation over levels) applies equally to interpreting the resulting spillover matrix. A network-aware check (e.g. correlating against each receiver’s weighted exposure through all sources, not just the direct source-receiver pair) would be needed to test this properly; that is follow-up work, not a fix to spillover_sanity_checks() as specified.
